Surah al-Takwir is Meccan, and its verses number twenty-nine.

﴿When the sun is wrapped up﴾. That is: it is folded up, from kawwartu al-'imamah (I wound the turban) when I wrap it. The meaning of this may be either its removal and displacement from its place, for when a garment is to be lifted it is rolled up and folded, and similar to this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿On the Day We will roll up the heaven﴾. Or it may mean the folding up of its light, which spreads out over the horizons and extends through the regions, so that this is a metaphor for its removal and its being taken away, by way of the principle that the cessation of what is necessarily connected ensures the cessation of what it is connected to. Or it means that it was thrown down from its orbit, just as the stars are described as inkidar (falling), from ta'anahu fa-kawwarahu (he struck him and threw him down), when he cast him onto the ground. And from Abu Salih: kuwwirat means nukkisat (it was overturned). And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, its takwir means its being made to enter the Throne. The root of the construction revolves around circling and gathering. The word al-shams (the sun) is in the nominative case as the subject of a verb understood, which the mentioned verb explains. According to some, it is in the nominative as the subject of a new sentence (mubtada').

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 81, verse 2:

﴿And when the stars fall, scattering﴾. That is: they fall down (inqaddat, "to be dispersed/to plunge"; in the sense of inqadda, "to fall"). It is also said: they scatter and drop down. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, that on that Day no star will remain except that it falls to the earth. And from him, may Allah be pleased with him, that the stars are lamps suspended between the heaven and the earth by chains of light, in the hands of angels made of light; so when those in the heavens and those on the earth die, they will fall from the hands of these (angels). It is also said: their inkidar (dispersal) is the extinguishing of their light. And it is narrated that the sun and the stars will be cast into Hell so that those who worshipped them may see them, as He says: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are fuel for Hell﴾.
﴿And when the mountains are set in motion﴾: that is, removed from their places by the quaking that takes place, not in the air, for that occurs after the second blast.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 81, verse 4:

(p-115) ﴿And when the pregnant she-camels are neglected﴾. ʿIshar is the plural of ʿushara’ (the pregnant she-camel), which is the one whose pregnancy has reached ten months; this is its name until it gives birth at the completion of the year. She is the most precious thing to her people and the dearest of their possessions to them.

﴿ʿuṭṭilat﴾: they are left unattended, because their owners are preoccupied with themselves. It is also said: ʿishar means the clouds, for the Arabs liken them to the pregnant (female). From this is the saying of God Most High: ﴿And the burdened clouds (al-ḥāmilāt wiqran)﴾. Their being neglected (taʿṭīl) means their not raining. It has also been read as "ʿuṭilat" with a light (unstressed) pronunciation.

And when the wild beasts are gathered together (﴿وَإذا الوُحُوشُ حُشِرَتْ﴾). That is: they are brought together from every direction. It has also been said: they are raised up for retribution. Qatadah said: every creature will be gathered, even the flies, for retribution. When judgment has been passed between them, they will be returned to dust, and none will remain of them except what brings joy to the children of Adam and admiration for its form, such as the peacock and the like. It is also read "ḥushshirat" with the doubled letter (shaddah).

﴿And when the seas are set ablaze﴾. That is: they are made to blaze, or they are filled by the bursting of some of them into others, until they become one single sea. It is from "sajara al-tannur" (he filled the oven with firewood so as to heat it). It was also said: they are filled with fires blazing to torment the people of the Fire. And it is narrated from al-Hasan that their water will vanish until not a drop remains in them. It is also read "sujirat" with the lighter pronunciation.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 81, verse 7:

﴿And when the souls are paired﴾ That is: they are joined to their bodies; or each soul is joined with its like (shakl); or with its record (kitab); or with its deeds ('amal); or the souls of the believers are joined with the wide-eyed maidens (hur), and the souls of the disbelievers with the devils (shayatin).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 81, verse 8:

﴿And when the buried-alive girl is asked﴾ That is: the one buried alive. The Arabs used to bury their daughters alive for fear of poverty or of the shame that would fall upon them because of them. It is said that when a man among them had a daughter born to him, he would dress her in a woollen or hair garment, until she reached six years of age. Then he would take her to the desert, where he had dug a pit for her, and he would throw her into it and shovel dirt over her. It is also said: when a pregnant woman drew near her time, she would dig a pit and labour over the edge of the pit. If she gave birth to a girl, she would throw her into it; and if she gave birth to a boy, she would keep him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 81, verse 9:

﴿When the girl buried alive is asked﴾ ﴿for what sin she was killed﴾. The address of the question to her is for her consolation, and to show complete anger and indignation toward her killers, and to lower him (the one who buried her) from the rank of being addressed, and to intensify his rebuke, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah?"﴾. It has also been read as "sa'alat" (she demanded/ sued), meaning she disputed, or as "sa'alat" (she asked) Allah the Exalted, or her killer. The phrase "qutilat" (she was killed) is used because the speech is a report about her, not a quotation of what she was addressed with when she was asked, so that it would be said "qutilti" (you were killed) in the second person, nor a quotation of her own words when she asked, so that it would be said "qutiltu" (I was killed) in the first person as a report of herself. It has also been read thus with the intensive form (qutthilat). It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he was asked about the children of the polytheists, and he said they will not be punished, and he cited this verse as evidence.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 81, verse 10:

﴿And when the scrolls are unrolled﴾ That is: the scrolls of deeds, for they are folded up at death and unfolded at the reckoning. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "People will be gathered naked and barefoot." Umm Salama said: "What about the women?" He said: "People will be preoccupied, O Umm Salama." She said: "And what will preoccupy them?" He said: "The unrolling of the scrolls, in which are the weights of atoms (mathaqil al-dharr) and the weights of mustard seeds (mathaqil al-khardal)." It has also been said: "unrolled" means "distributed" among their owners. And it is related from Marthad ibn Wada'a that on the Day of Resurrection the scrolls will fly out from beneath the Throne, so the scroll of the believer will fall into his hand in a lofty Garden, and the scroll of the disbeliever will fall into his hand amid scorching wind (samum) and boiling water (hamim). That is: what is written in them is that, and these are scrolls other than the scrolls of deeds.

And when the sky is stripped away (﴿وَإذا السَّماءُ كُشِطَتْ﴾). It is cut off and removed, just as the hide is stripped from a slaughtered animal, and as a covering is removed from the thing that is covered by it. It has also been read as "qashatat" (قَشَطَتْ), and the interchange of the kaf and the qaf is not rare, as in al-kafur and al-qafur.

﴿And when the Hellfire is kindled﴾: that is, it is set ablaze with intense fire. It is said that the anger of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and the sins of the children of Adam kindled it. It was also read as "suʿirat" (سُعِرَتْ) with lightening (takhfif, reading without doubling the letter).

The Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 81, verse 13:

﴿And when Paradise is brought near﴾ — i.e., it is brought near to the God-fearing, as in His saying, ﴿And Paradise will be brought near to the God-fearing, not far off﴾. It has been said: these are twelve matters, six of which are in this world, i.e., between the two blastings, and these are from the beginning of the surah to His saying, ﴿And when the seas are set ablaze﴾, on the basis that what is meant by the gathering of the wild beasts is bringing them together from every quarter so that I may resurrect them for retribution; and six are in the Hereafter, i.e., after the second blast.

And the Most High's saying, ﴿a soul will know what it has brought forward﴾, is the answer to "idha" (when). Its meaning is a single extended period of time that encompasses what is in its context and the context of the characteristics joined to it. It begins with the first blast (al-nafkha al-ula), and it ends with the decisive judgment between the creatures (fasl al-qada'). However, this does not mean that the soul knows what it knows in every part of that long period, or at the occurrence of one of those calamities, but rather at the spreading out of the pages (nashr al-suhuf). Yet, since some of those calamities are at its beginnings and some are among its consequences, the knowledge of them is attributed to the time of the occurrence of all of them, to magnify the matter and to make the situation appear dreadful. By "what it has brought forward" is meant its deeds, good and bad. Its "bringing forward" is either the presence of its pages, as the spreading out of them indicates, or the presence of the souls themselves, according to what they have said: that the outward deeds in this life take on an accidental form, which appears in the next life in substantial forms suitable to them in goodness and ugliness, in specific modes and determined configurations, to the extent that sins and disobediences take on bodily form there and appear in the shape of fire. On this is interpreted the Most High's saying, ﴿Indeed, Hell is surrounding the disbelievers﴾, and His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who consume the wealth of orphans unjustly are only consuming fire into their bellies﴾, and likewise the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning one who drinks from vessels of gold and silver: "He is only swallowing the fire of Hell into his belly." (p-117) There is no remoteness in this, for do you not see that knowledge appears in the world of similitude (alam al-mithal) in the form of milk, as is not hidden from one who has experience with the conditions of the Five Divine Presences (al-hadarat al-khams)? It has been related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the good deeds will be brought forth in a beautiful form and the evil deeds in an ugly form, and they will be placed in the scale. Whatever the case, attributing their bringing forward to the soul, although it is brought forward by the command of Allah the Most High, as His saying indicates, ﴿the Day every soul will find what it has done of good present﴾, etc., is because it, having done them in the world, is as if it had brought them forward at the station of standing. The meaning of its knowledge of them at that time is that it witnesses them as they truly are. If it is righteous, it witnesses them in forms more beautiful than those in which it witnessed them in the world, because acts of obedience are never free of some kind of hardship. If it is evil, it witnesses them in contrast to how it witnessed them here, because it had been adorning them for it, agreeing with its desire. The indefiniteness of "soul" (nafs), which conveys that the stated knowledge is for an individual soul or for some of them, is to announce that its being established for all of its individuals, entirely, is so manifest and clear that hardly any trace of doubt can hover around it, a certainty every person knows, even if one were to bring an expression indicating the opposite. And it also alludes to the fact that those souls which know what has been mentioned, even with their multitude and the abundance of their numbers, are considered small in relation to the majesty of the Greatness, to which allusion is made to some of the wonders of His affairs, which indicate the magnitude of His dominion. As for what has been said, that this is of the kind of reversal of speech ('aks al-kalam), in which one intends by it excessiveness in what is reversed from it, and its illustration by the Most High's saying, ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾, and by the saying of one who said:

"I may leave the opponent with his fingertips yellowed,"

and by the saying of one who said when asked about the number of his horsemen:

"Many a horseman is with me, and with him are the troops,"

intending by that the excess in increasing his horsemen and showing his innocence of exaggeration, and that he is one who minimizes what he has much of, let alone exaggerating it, then this is among the clear indications of noble reflection. However, the reversed speech in what has been mentioned of the examples is something that admits excessiveness and exaggeration in it, for in the first case one often wishes, and in the second one often leaves, and in the third there are many horsemen, and each of these is capable of excess and hyperbole in it, because the degrees of abundance are not limited. And by its reversal what has been mentioned of excessive increase was intended, according to what is evident. As for what we are dealing with, the speech from which it is reversed is "a soul will know what it has brought forward," as the speaker stated, and there is no possibility of increase in it so that by its reversal exaggeration and excess in it would be intended. What is possible in it of exaggeration is what we have mentioned, so reflect. It is also possible that this is to indicate that when a soul among the souls knows at that time what it has brought forward, it becomes obligatory upon every soul to reform its deeds, out of fear that it may be the very one that knows what it has brought forward. So how much more so when every soul knows it, in the manner of your saying to one whom you advise: "Perhaps you will regret what you have done." Often a person regrets what he has done, yet you do not intend by this that his regret is hoped for to exist, not certain, or rarely occurring. Rather, you mean that the sensible person must avoid a matter in which regret is hoped for or rarely fails to occur. So how much more so when it is of certain existence and frequent occurrence.

﴿So I swear by the stars that recede﴾. That is, the receding stars (al-kawakib al-rawajie), from khanasa, meaning "he withdrew" or "he fell back" when he delayed. They are the five planets other than the two luminaries (al-nayyirayn), namely Bahram (Mars), Zuhal (Saturn), Utarid (Mercury), al-Zuhra (Venus), and al-Mushtari (Jupiter). They were described by His saying, may He be exalted: *

(p-118) ﴿The planets that run and hide﴾ — because they move along with the sun and the moon, and they recede until they are concealed beneath the light of the sun. So their khunus (receding) is their returning, and their kunus (hiding) is their being concealed beneath its light, from the expression kanasa al-wahshiyyu (the wild animal entered its kinās), when it entered its kinās, which is the shelter it makes from the branches of trees. It has been said: it refers to all the stars, which recede (takhnisu) by day and so disappear from sight, and hide (taknisu) by night, meaning they rise in their places like wild animals in their kunus (lairs).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 81, verse 17:

﴿And by the night when it turns its back (ʿasʿasa)﴾: that is, its darkness has either retreated or advanced, for it is among the words with opposite meanings (aḍdad), and likewise ʿasʿasa. Al-Farrāʾ said: The commentators have agreed that the meaning of ʿasʿasa is "it turned its back" (adbara). Evidence for this is the verse of al-ʿAjjāj:

؎ Until, when the dawn breathed upon it, ∗∗∗ and its night withdrew from it and ʿasʿasa

It was also said: it is a dialect specific to the Quraysh. And it was said: the meaning of the advance of its darkness (iqbāluhu) is more fitting to His, the Exalted's, saying: *

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 81, verse 18:

﴿By the dawn when it breathes out﴾ because it is the beginning of the day. And it has been said: its turning away (idbaruhu) is closer to the breathing out of the dawn (tanaffus al-subh). Its meaning is: when the dawn approaches, with its approach there comes a refreshing breeze and a gentle wind; so that is made a "breath" for it, metaphorically (majazan), and it is said, "the dawn breathed out" (tanaffasa al-subhu).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 81, verse 19:

﴿Indeed, it﴾ i.e., the noble Qur'an, which speaks of the terrible calamities mentioned above.

﴿is the word of a noble messenger﴾ and he is Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him, who uttered it on behalf of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 81, verse 20:

﴿Possessing strength﴾, intense, like His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Mighty in power﴾. It has also been said: what is meant is strength in performing the obedience of Allah, exalted be He, and not falling short in it, from the beginning of creation to the end of the period of moral responsibility (taklif).

﴿In the presence of the Lord of the Throne, held in high esteem﴾: possessing a lofty rank with Allah, exalted be He. The "presence" here is one of honour and dignity, not a presence of place.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 81, verse 21:

﴿Obeyed﴾ among his noble angels; they issue forth from his command and return to his judgment.

﴿Trustworthy﴾ with the revelation. "Thumma" (then) is an adverb of time/rank referring to what precedes it, and it was said that it refers to what follows it. It was also recited as "thumma," to magnify the quality of trustworthiness and to give it precedence over the other qualities.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 81, verse 22:

﴿And your companion is not(ـ) ﴾ is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

﴿Mad﴾, as the disbelievers slander him, and the reference to the title of companionship is to allude to their being fully acquainted with the details of his circumstances (peace be upon him) through experience, and their knowledge of his purity (peace be upon him) from what they attributed to him entirely. It has been used as evidence for the virtue of Jibril (peace be upon both of them) because of the clear contrast between their two attributes, but this is weak, since the purpose is to refute the claim of the disbelievers concerning him (peace be upon him) that he is merely taught by a human, one who fabricates lies against Allah, or that there is madness in him? It is not a enumeration of their virtues nor a comparison.

(p-119) ﴿And he indeed saw him﴾ — that is: by Allah, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ indeed saw Jibril, peace and blessings be upon them both.

﴿On the clear horizon﴾ — at the rising-place of the sun, the highest (one).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 81, verse 24:

﴿And he is not﴾, i.e., the Messenger of Allah ﷺ,

﴿over the unseen﴾, over what he conveys of the revelation sent to him and other unseen matters.

﴿with a miser﴾, i.e., not stingy, one who does not withhold the revelation and does not fall short in conveying and teaching. It is also read as "bi-zanin" (بِظَنِينٍ), i.e., accused, from al-zinna (الظِّنَّة), which is accusation.

The passage is short; translating it faithfully:

﴿And it is not the word of an accursed devil.﴾ That is, the word of one of the eavesdroppers upon the heavenly message (al-mustariqah lil-sam‘, i.e. those who steal hearing), and this is a negation of their claim that it is soothsaying (kihanah) and sorcery (sihr).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 81, verse 26:

﴿Where then are you going?﴾ This is a question seeking to make them lose their way (istidlal, a rhetorical question asking them to justify) regarding what they pursue concerning the matter of the Qur'an. The fa' (the particle "then") indicates the sequence of what follows it upon what precedes it, namely the clarity that it is a manifest revelation, and it has nothing to do with what they say. It is like when you say to someone who has left the main road after it has become clear: "This is the clear path, so where are you going?"

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 81, verse 27:

﴿It is not﴾ meaning: it is not.

﴿except a reminder to the worlds﴾ meaning: an admonition and a reminding for them.

Her Lord's words, ﴿for whoever among you wills to go straight﴾, are a substitution (badal) for "the worlds" (al-'alamin), with the preposition repeated. His words, ﴿to go straight﴾ (an yastaqim), are the object of "wills" (shaa), meaning: for whoever among you wills uprightness (al-istiqamah) by seeking out the truth (taharri al-haqq) and persistently adhering to what is correct (mulazamat al-sawab). Its substitution for "the worlds" is because they are the ones who benefit from the reminder (al-tadhkir).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 81, verse 29:

﴿وَما تَشاءُونَ﴾ That is: [You do not will] uprightness, with a will that is followed by it at some time or other.

﴿إلا أنْ يَشاءَ اللَّهُ﴾ That is: except at the time when Allah Most High wills that will, namely the will that is followed by uprightness. For your will is not followed by it without Allah Most High's will for it.

﴿رَبُّ العالَمِينَ﴾ The Master of all creation and its Nourisher, all of them.

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah at-Takwir, Allah will protect him from being disgraced when his record is spread open."
